transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

When there’s a line or a process, I just can’t seem to wait my turn without jumping ahead or changing plans, and it keeps messing up our money and appointments. It’s gotten so bad that my wife and our parish priest urged me to come in before we lose our housing.
Can you tell me more about what happens when you try to focus on a task or sit still for a period of time, do you find yourself getting easily distracted or restless?

Yes, it's a major struggle because when I try to focus on paperwork or bills, my mind quickly drifts off to a song in my head or the birds outside and I have to keep restarting. Plus, trying to sit still at home or in church gives me this buzzing feeling inside, so I'm constantly bouncing my legs, tapping my fingers, or needing to get up and pace around because sitting still feels almost impossible.

Can you describe a recent situation where you acted on impulse without thinking it through, such as interrupting others, blurting out answers, or doing something on the spur of the moment that might have caused problems?

When I'm talking to the lady at the housing office or in meetings for our church food pantry, I find myself jumping in and finishing people's sentences before they can even finish explaining. Because I blurt things out like that, I often realize too late that I didn't actually listen to the whole question. It ends up causing problems because I'll give the wrong information or agree to things I don't really understand.

Can you tell me more about how often you experience physical restlessness, such as fidgeting or feeling the need to get up and move around, versus acting on impulse without thinking, like blurting out answers or interrupting others?

Honestly, both of these things happen almost constantly and cause me a lot of trouble. Physically, I always have this buzzing inside that makes me fidget, bounce my legs, or get up to pace around during important appointments because sitting still feels like being trapped. At the same time, I'm constantly blurting out answers, finishing people's sentences, and struggling so much in lines that I try to jump ahead or just walk away.

Can you compare how often you experience impulsivity, such as blurting out answers or interrupting others, to how often you feel the need to be physically active or fidgety, and which one of these symptoms seems to cause you more distress or problems in your daily life?

Both happen constantly—I always have a buzzing inside that makes me fidget and bounce my legs, and I'm always blurting out answers and interrupting people. But the impulsivity causes much more distress because jumping out of lines and making hasty decisions directly lead to errors on forms and missed financial benefits, which is putting my family at risk of losing our home.

Can you tell me if there was ever a period in your life, such as during childhood, when these symptoms of impulsivity and restlessness were less of a problem, or have they been consistently present and troublesome for you as long as you can remember?

These issues have actually been with me since childhood; back in elementary school, teachers constantly called my mom because I couldn't stay in my seat, blurted things out, and got sent to the hallway. It was less of a disaster back then and during my early adult life because I had loose, informal jobs and family to quietly redirect me, but the underlying restlessness has always been there.

You mentioned that these symptoms have been present since childhood, but can you help me understand if there was ever a period, even a short one, where these symptoms significantly improved or decreased, perhaps during adolescence or early adulthood, before they became as problematic as they are now?

No, the symptoms themselves never actually improved or went away when I was younger. It’s just that they didn't cause as many problems back then because my constant movement and impulsive choices were absorbed by informal jobs and church activities where the structure was loose and people quietly redirected me. It only became a severe issue about two years ago when I had to start managing tight budgets, paperwork, and strict appointments.

Can you describe how your symptoms of impulsivity and restlessness impact your ability to maintain employment or engage in activities that require sustained mental effort, and are there any specific situations where one symptom seems to overshadow the other in terms of causing problems?

The constant buzzing and need to move make sitting through meetings or doing paperwork nearly impossible, which has kept me from getting a steady job like the community-center aide position I've tried for. When I'm alone trying to focus on bills, that physical restlessness takes over completely, but when I'm interacting with others, my impulsivity and jumping ahead completely overshadows it and causes immediate, severe financial damage.

Can you clarify if your impulsivity, such as blurting out answers or interrupting others, tends to occur more frequently in situations where you're under pressure or stressed, versus your physical restlessness and need to move, which seems to be present regardless of the situation?

I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really tracked if the blurting out happens more when I'm stressed compared to the restlessness. I just know that both of them happen a whole lot and cause me a ton of trouble every single day.

Can you tell me if you've noticed any significant differences in how often or severely you experience impulsivity versus physical restlessness when you're in highly structured environments, like a traditional office setting, compared to less structured ones, like working from home or being outdoors?

I've actually never worked in a traditional office setting or worked from home, since I've mostly done informal jobs and am not currently in the workforce. Because of that, I'm really not sure how to compare those specific environments. I just know how much I struggle in places like the benefits office, at church, or at home.

Can you estimate how much of your daily distress or problems is caused by your impulsivity, such as blurting out answers, versus how much is caused by your physical restlessness, like fidgeting or needing to move around?

Both of them cause immense trouble, just in different ways. The impulsivity causes the most direct, severe damage because blurting things out and jumping ahead leads to immediate mistakes with our money and missed benefits. But the physical restlessness is what makes the day-to-day struggle of waiting in offices or sitting through meetings feel agonizing and almost impossible to endure.

Can you think of any situation where you were able to control your physical restlessness, such as fidgeting, but still found yourself acting impulsively, like blurting out answers or interrupting others?

I can't really recall a specific time when I managed to keep my body perfectly still but still ended up blurting things out or interrupting. Usually, both the physical restlessness and the impulse to speak or act without thinking tend to happen at the exact same time. They just seem to go hand-in-hand for me.

Can you describe a situation where you were able to manage your impulsivity, such as waiting for your turn to speak, but still struggled with physical restlessness, like fidgeting or needing to get up and move around?

It is very hard for me to separate the two, and I can't really think of a time where I successfully controlled my impulsivity while only struggling with physical restlessness. Usually, when I feel that physical restlessness and buzzing inside, the impulsive actions happen right along with it. That makes it extremely difficult to manage either one of them.
Do you find that your physical restlessness tends to precede your impulsive behaviors, or do they seem to occur simultaneously without one clearly triggering the other?

I’m not quite sure about that, and I haven't really thought about it that way before. When I'm in the moment, the restlessness and the urge to act feel like they hit me all at once, making it hard to tell if one triggers the other.
Can you think of any times when you felt extremely restless but managed to wait and think before acting, or does the restlessness always seem to lead to impulsive decisions?

That buzzing feeling of restlessness almost always leads directly to me acting without thinking. When I get that extreme impatience while waiting, it feels nearly impossible to hold back. I almost always end up jumping ahead, changing my plans, or making a hasty decision right then and there.
Can you describe a situation where you experienced a significant reduction in either your impulsivity or your physical restlessness, and if so, which one improved and under what circumstances?

I haven't really ever experienced a situation where my restlessness or impulsivity significantly improved or went away. They have always been there, though they didn't cause as much trouble in the past when I was doing active, informal jobs or church activities where I could move around freely.
Can you think of any specific triggers or situations where your impulsivity, such as blurting out answers, seems to happen without the physical restlessness, or are they always intertwined for you?

I'm not quite sure, and I haven't really thought about whether they happen separately from each other. It usually just feels like my mind and my body are both constantly racing and on the go at the exact same time.
Can you describe any differences in how your symptoms of impulsivity and physical restlessness are affected by the presence of others, such as in social situations versus when you are alone?

I haven't really noticed a major difference or thought about how it varies when I'm alone versus with other people. The restlessness and impatience feel pretty constant either way. It just seems like my body and mind are always racing regardless of who is around.

Can you tell me if you've ever experienced a period where one of these symptoms, either the impulsivity or the physical restlessness, was significantly more prominent than the other, and if so, what was happening during that time?

I'm not really sure, and I haven't thought about it that way before. For me, the physical restlessness and the impulsive decisions have always seemed to go hand-in-hand, especially over the last couple of years as the pressure at home has built up.

Looking back over the past few years, have you noticed if there are times when your impulsivity, such as blurting out answers, seems to overshadow your physical restlessness, or vice versa, and if so, under what circumstances does this happen?

I haven't really thought about whether one overshadows the other, as both the physical restlessness and the impulsivity feel very constant and troublesome for me. They often happen at the same time, depending on whether I am trying to sit still or having a conversation with someone. Both of them just seem to cause me a lot of stress all the time.

Can you think of any situations where managing one symptom, either your impulsivity or your physical restlessness, made it easier to manage the other, or do they always seem to affect each other equally?

Honestly, I haven't really figured out how to manage either of them yet, so I'm not sure if managing one would help with the other. They both just seem to happen at the exact same time and feel pretty overwhelming to deal with.

Can you tell me if you have ever experienced any periods of significant improvement or reduction in your symptoms, either impulsivity or physical restlessness, in response to any treatments, lifestyle changes, or environmental factors?

I haven't ever undergone any treatment, and I haven't found any lifestyle changes that make the restlessness or impulsivity go away. In the past, when I had fewer responsibilities and a much looser schedule, the symptoms were still there but they just didn't cause as many problems.

Can you compare how much your impulsivity, such as blurting out answers, interferes with your daily life and relationships versus how much your physical restlessness, like fidgeting, does, and which one do you think is more of a challenge for you to manage on a daily basis?

While my physical restlessness is constant—like my bouncing legs, tapping fingers, and needing to pace during long waits, which gets me weird looks in church—it mostly just makes me feel trapped. The impulsivity is definitely the bigger challenge because blurting out answers and jumping ahead in lines leads to me giving wrong information and losing my spot, which has caused real financial harm to my family.
Can you think of any situation where you felt the urge to act impulsively, but were able to control it and wait, and if so, what helped you to do so?

I honestly can't think of any recent situations where I was successfully able to control the urge and wait. It feels like the impulse almost always wins out, especially lately. That's really why it has been causing so many problems with our money and appointments.
Can you estimate the percentage of times when you feel the urge to act impulsively that you are also experiencing significant physical restlessness, and vice versa?

I'm really not sure of an exact percentage, and I've never actually tracked it or thought about it that way. I just know that the physical restlessness and those impulsive urges seem to happen together very often, almost every time.

Do you often find yourself making careless mistakes or having difficulty sustaining attention in tasks, such as when doing paperwork or bills, and does this happen more frequently than your impulsive behaviors?

Yes, I have a lot of trouble staying focused on paperwork or bills; my mind just drifts off to the birds outside or a song in my head, and I constantly have to restart because I lose my place. I'm not entirely sure which happens more frequently, though, because both my attention struggles and my impulsive behaviors are constantly causing major problems for me.

Can you tell me more about how often you find yourself making careless mistakes or having difficulty sustaining attention in tasks, and does this happen as frequently as your impulsive behaviors or physical restlessness?

Whenever I try to focus on bills or forms, my mind drifts off to the birds outside or a song in my head after just a few minutes, and I lose my place completely. While the physical urge to fidget and jump ahead is a constant, daily struggle, these focus issues are just as frequent and destructive whenever I am forced to sit down and do paperwork.

Can you clarify if there are specific situations or contexts where your impulsivity causes more problems than your physical restlessness, or if there are times when the restlessness is more bothersome, and how do these situations differ?

My impulsivity causes the most actual damage in official settings, like when I blurt out wrong answers in housing meetings or jump out of lines and lose our spot. On the other hand, the physical restlessness is most bothersome during quiet, stationary moments, like when I feel a buzzing inside and have to pace while doing paperwork or helping my son with homework.

You've mentioned that these symptoms have been present since childhood, but can you clarify if they have been consistently problematic throughout your life, or if there were periods where they were less severe or caused fewer problems?

For most of my life, they didn't cause major problems because I had informal jobs and church activities where things were relaxed and people quietly redirected me. It only became a severe, constant disaster about two years ago when I had to take on strict responsibilities like managing our tight budget, filling out paperwork, and keeping official appointments.

Can you describe how your symptoms of impulsivity and physical restlessness have affected your daily life and relationships, and which one of these symptoms do you feel has had the most significant impact on your overall well-being?

My physical restlessness, like constantly bouncing my legs and needing to pace, has really strained my relationship with my wife and our parish priest. However, the impulsivity—specifically my inability to wait my turn and acting before thinking—has had the most devastating impact because it directly threatens my family's housing and financial survival.
